blocks.explanation:
An equation in which the unknown \(n\) is the top number of two combinations.
We must find \(n\).
Plan: use the rule: if \({}^{n}C_{x} = {}^{n}C_{y}\) then \(x = y\) or \(x + y = n\).
steps:
Given: \({}^{n}C_{6} = {}^{n}C_{2}\).
To find: \(n\).
Method: complementary combinations \({}^{n}C_{r} = {}^{n}C_{n-r}\) (Section 7.4.2). So equal combinations with the same \(n\) have equal lower numbers, or lower numbers that add up to \(n\).

Apply the rule
\[6 \ne 2\]
\[\Rightarrow 6 + 2 = n\]
\[n = 8\]
Why: The lower numbers are not equal, so they must be complementary: \(2 = n - 6\).

Check
\[{}^{8}C_{6} = {}^{8}C_{2}\]
\[= \dfrac{8 \cdot 7}{2} = 28\]
Why: Both sides give 28, because choosing 6 of 8 is the same as leaving out 2 of 8.

blocks.explanation:
The right side is not written as a combination yet.
We must find \(n\).
Plan: recognise the right side as \({}^{14}C_{3}\), turn it into \({}^{14}C_{11}\), then compare.
steps:
Given: \({}^{n}C_{11} = \frac{14 \cdot 13 \cdot 12}{3!}\).
To find: \(n\).
Method: \({}^{n}C_{r}\) = (\(r\) numbers counting down from \(n\)) \(\div\, r!\). Then use \({}^{n}C_{r} = {}^{n}C_{n-r}\).

Recognise the right side
\[\dfrac{14 \cdot 13 \cdot 12}{3!} = {}^{14}C_{3}\]
Why: Three numbers counting down from 14, divided by \(3!\), is exactly \({}^{14}C_{3}\).

Compare
\[{}^{n}C_{11} = {}^{14}C_{11}\]
\[n = 14\]
Why: The lower numbers are the same, so the upper numbers must be the same (for \(n \ge 11\), \({}^{n}C_{11}\) grows as \(n\) grows, so only one \(n\) works).

Check
\[\dfrac{14 \cdot 13 \cdot 12}{6} = \dfrac{2184}{6} = 364\]
\[{}^{14}C_{11} = {}^{14}C_{3} = 364 \;\checkmark\]
Why: Both sides are the same number.

blocks.explanation:
Same type as part (i): two equal combinations with the same top number \(n\).
We must find \(n\).
Plan: the lower numbers 5 and 10 are different, so they add up to \(n\).
steps:
Apply the rule
\[5 \ne 10\]
\[\Rightarrow n = 5 + 10 = 15\]
Why: The lower numbers are complementary: \(10 = n - 5\).
